Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Ana had always been proud of her independence, working as an HVAC technician in a male-dominated field and living alone in a small apartment. But it was this same independence that made her feel so vulnerable on the day she was taken by her ex-partner's associates and tortured for hours. The memory of those events still feels like it belongs to someone else, but the shame and overwhelm that come flooding back whenever it resurfaces are all too real. As Ana recalls the sound of the door slamming shut behind her, she can feel her heart racing and her senses go on high alert. She wakes up in the middle of the night, convinced that someone is breaking in, and has to get out of bed to check that the doors and windows are locked - a ritual she's performed countless times since the incident. Her friends and family have grown used to her constant checking, but Ana knows it's not just about being safe; it's about feeling like she can never truly be prepared for what might happen next. Being alone with women is another trigger that sets off this chain reaction of hypervigilance. Ana has started avoiding social gatherings where she might find herself in one-on-one situations with female friends or acquaintances, fearing that they might inadvertently remind her of the event or, worse still, be hiding malicious intentions. Her job requires her to interact with people all day, but even there, she finds herself scanning for potential threats - a glance at a coworker's injured hand and suddenly she's back in that room, feeling helpless and trapped. Ana has come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, and this fear has taken hold of her daily life. She doubts her own judgment, wondering if she'll make the wrong decision or trust the wrong person. Her self-doubt is suffocating at times, making it hard for her to concentrate on even simple tasks. As a result, she's started to notice changes in herself - withdrawal from friends and family, difficulty sleeping, an increasing reliance on avoidance behaviors to cope with the memories that haunt her. The more Ana tries to push these thoughts away, the more they seem to seep into every aspect of her life. She'll be working on a project when suddenly she's overcome by emotion, remembering the feeling of being trapped and powerless. It's as if the memory itself is trying to tell her something - that she's permanently changed for the worse, that she can never go back to who she was before. Ana feels like she's living in a state of constant alert, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. Lately, Ana has been struggling to keep up with her work and social obligations. She's started to notice how much more easily startled she is - a sudden noise or unexpected movement can send her heart racing all over again. The cycle feels endless: memories trigger fear, which in turn fuels more negative appraisals about herself and the world around her. Ana knows she needs help breaking this cycle, but it's hard for her to shake off the feeling that she's beyond repair. It was a particularly rough night, waking up multiple times to check on imaginary intruders, that finally brought Ana to seek professional help. As she sat in her apartment, waiting for dawn to break, she realized that she couldn't keep living like this - constantly looking over her shoulder, always expecting the worst. She wants to learn how to quiet these fears and take back control of her life, but most of all, she hopes to find a way to forgive herself for not being able to escape what happened to her.
